paragraphs.text: Familial adult myoclonic epilepsy-2 (FAME2) is an autosomal dominant disorder characterized by shivering-like tremor of cortical origin (cortical myoclonic tremor), myoclonus, and epilepsy (Striano et al., 2004; Madia et al., 2008). Henden et al. (2016) described FAME as a rare disorder with adult onset, involuntary muscle jerks, cortical myoclonus, and occasional seizures, and noted that it is genetically heterogeneous, with more than 70 families reported worldwide and 5 potential disease loci. Corbett et al. (2019) described FAME as characterized by cortical myoclonic tremor and overt myoclonic and later generalized tonic-clonic seizures, with onset in the second to third decade, variable expressivity within and between families, and anticipation in some families; seizures are typically controlled with antiepileptic drugs for generalized epilepsies, although drug resistance occurs rarely.

paragraphs.text: Guerrini et al. (2001) described a pedigree with 8 affected individuals who had a nonprogressive disorder beginning between ages 12 and 50 years. All patients had predominantly distal, semicontinuous rhythmic myoclonus and generalized tonic-clonic seizures, and 3 had complex partial seizures. Most rarely had seizures and had normal cognition, but 3 with intractable seizures had mild mental retardation. All affected members had frontotemporal as well as generalized interictal EEG abnormalities. Neurophysiologic studies suggested a cortical origin of the myoclonus: back-averaging showed EEG waves whose frequency matched the EMG bursts. In 5 patients, EMG and EEG over the contralateral rolandic area showed significant coherence at 8 to 25 Hz, with EEG activity preceding EMG activity by 8 to 15 ms, and in 2 individuals ipsilateral EEG-EMG coherence was consistent with transcallosal spread of myoclonic activity. Patients had an enhanced C-reflex at rest and high-amplitude somatosensory and visual evoked potentials. Compared with controls, patients had a significantly reduced resting motor threshold to transcranial magnetic stimulation (38%) and a significantly shorter post-motor evoked potential silent period (101 ms vs 137 ms in controls). The authors suggested that these findings reflect diffuse cortical hyperexcitability particularly involving frontotemporal circuits.

paragraphs.text: Striano et al. (2005) reported a 5-generation family from Naples, Italy, with cortical tremor, myoclonus, and epilepsy. Eleven members, aged 24 to 56 years (mean 39.2 years), had hand tremor and myoclonus, and 6 of them also had generalized seizures. Electrophysiologic study confirmed cortical reflex myoclonus in all affected members. Giant somatosensory evoked potential components and an enhanced long loop reflex I were found in 3 presymptomatic family members, who developed hand tremor and upper-limb myoclonus after 1.5 years of follow-up.

paragraphs.text: Suppa et al. (2009) described an Italian family with familial cortical myoclonic tremor with epilepsy (FCMTE). Clinically affected members had limb and voice tremor, seizures, and myoclonus of the eyelids during blinking. Neuropsychological testing showed visuospatial impairment, which the authors suggested might be due to temporal lobe dysfunction. Neurophysiologic findings suggested increased excitability of the primary motor cortex with normal sensorimotor integration.

paragraphs.text: Coppola et al. (2011) evaluated clinical, electrophysiologic, and treatment data on 14 patients from 3 families with autosomal dominant cortical tremor, myoclonus, and epilepsy linked to chromosome 2p11.1-q12.2. Mean age at onset was 20.2 years (range 11 to 40 years), and mean follow-up was 14.0 years. Myoclonus worsened gradually in 10 patients (71.4%), and its severity correlated with disease duration and patient age; 2 patients older than 80 years had myoclonus that interfered with walking on their own. Six patients (42.8%) had seizures, usually between the second and sixth decades of life, and more than a third had psychiatric and neuropsychological dysfunction. Over the long term, EEG background activity slowed progressively as myoclonus worsened, whereas paroxysmal activity and photosensitivity were most evident in the intermediate phases of the disease. The authors concluded that the disorder shows slight age-dependent progression.

paragraphs.text: Crompton et al. (2012) described a 6-generation kindred of European descent with familial adult myoclonic epilepsy, ascertained in New Zealand and Australia. All 55 affected members had fine hand tremor, with onset typically in adolescence (median age 15 years; range 4-60 years). Proximal myoclonus was present in 44 of 55 (80%), arising later than the hand tremor (median 17 years; range 5-60 years), and generalized tonic-clonic seizures occurred in 8 of 55 (15%), with a median age at onset of 43.5 years (range 18-76 years). Neurophysiologic testing confirmed features of cortical reflex myoclonus. The authors concluded that the most common phenotype in this family was mild postural hand tremor resembling essential tremor combined with subtle proximal myoclonus; generalized tonic-clonic seizures were uncommon and occurred around sleep onset following severe generalized myoclonus.

paragraphs.text: Licchetta et al. (2013) described a large Italian family with FCMTE in which 25 of 127 members were affected (9 males, 16 females); 16 of the 19 living affected members were studied (mean age 47.8 years). Cortical myoclonic tremor was associated with generalized seizures in 10 patients (62.5%). Mean age at onset was 28.1 years for cortical myoclonic tremor and 33.8 years for seizures. Four patients (25%) reported slow progression of the tremor, with severe gait impairment in 1, and psychiatric disorders of variable severity occurred in 37.5% of cases. Polygraphic studies in 15 family members recorded rhythmic bursts at 7 to 15 Hz in all 11 affected members tested, and back-averaging and somatosensory evoked potentials with C-reflex studies in 4 showed a cortical origin of myoclonus in all patients tested. Generalized epileptiform discharges were recorded in 25% of cases and a photoparoxysmal response in 31%.

paragraphs.text: In affected members of 3 FAME2 families (Australian/New Zealand, Italian, and French/Spanish), Corbett et al. (2019) identified, by whole-genome sequencing with repeat-expansion detection, an expansion of an ATTTT repeat with insertion of an ATTTC repeat in intron 1 of the STARD7 gene. The ATTTC repeat was absent from 69 control genomes. By repeat-primed PCR, the expansion was found in a total of 158 affected individuals from 22 families, as well as in 1 of 52 unrelated singletons, and in 2 of 24 unaffected relatives, both from younger generations and likely presymptomatic; it was not amplified in 28 control DNA samples. Long-read sequencing showed the structure (AAATG)n[N](AAAAT)n on the forward strand, with reads in 1 patient containing 274 to 345 AAATG and 387 to 390 AAAAT repeats, suggesting somatic variability, and a read from another patient containing 588 AAATG and 340 AAAAT repeats (4,645 bp). STARD7 mRNA and protein levels were unchanged in patient fibroblasts.
